Decrease
de-krees'
v. (to grow less; the Baptist's own account of his ministry set against Christ's, and a mercy promised over a man's cattle)
From Latin decrescere, to grow less, from de- and crescere, to grow. The Greek at John 3:30 is elattoo, to make less; the Hebrew at Psalm 107:38 is maat, to become small or few.

Biblical Definition

The great occurrence is five words long: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). John the Baptist's disciples had come to him troubled that the crowds were going to Jesus, and this was his answer. He had already given the figure that explains it: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled” (John 3:29). The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and then stepped out of it; his whole office was to bring the two together, and his gladness came from hearing the bridegroom's voice, not from being heard himself. The must in verse 30 is a divine necessity, not a resolution John made — it was appointed that he should diminish. The only other occurrence is a quiet mercy in the psalm of the redeemed: God “blesseth them also, so that they are multiplied greatly; and suffereth not their cattle to decrease” (Psalm 107:38). The same God who appoints a man's decrease keeps a poor man's herd from dwindling.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines decrease as to become less, to be diminished gradually in extent, bulk, quantity, or amount.

expand to see more

DECREASE, v.i. To become less; to be diminished gradually, in extent, bulk, quantity, or amount, or in strength, quality or excellence.

He must increase, but I must decrease. John 3.

DECREASE, v.t. To lessen; to make smaller in dimensions, amount, quality or excellence.

DECREASE, n. A becoming less; gradual diminution; decay.

2. The wane of the moon; the wane or decline of the moon's illuminated part.

Key Scripture

John 3:30 — "He must increase, but I must decrease."

John 3:29 — "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled."

Psalm 107:38 — "He blesseth them also, so that they are multiplied greatly; and suffereth not their cattle to decrease."

John 3:27 — "John answered and said, A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven."

Modern Corruption

John 3:30 is used as a slogan for self-deprecation, when it is a statement about the structure of an office and the joy proper to it.

expand to see more

The verse has been reduced to a sentiment about personal humility, roughly equivalent to thinking less of oneself. John says something more definite and more freeing. He states the fact of an office: he is the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom, and a wedding does not go wrong when the best man leaves the couple alone — that is the wedding working. He also grounds the whole thing in a doctrine two verses earlier: a man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven. His decrease is not modesty about a ministry he owned; it is accuracy about a ministry he had been lent.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joy attached. John does not say I must decrease with resignation; he says this my joy therefore is fulfilled, and the fulfilment is in hearing the bridegroom's voice. A ministry, a parent, a teacher, or an older believer whose usefulness is visibly being succeeded by someone else can grieve the loss or can hear the voice. Our Lord's verdict on the man who spoke this sentence is that among them born of women there had not risen a greater. He decreased on schedule and lost nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek elattoo, to make or become less — John 3:30; auxano, to increase — the paired verb; dei, it is necessary — the divine must; Hebrew maat, to diminish — Psalm 107:38.

expand to see more

Greek elattoo — to make less, decrease; John 3:30, and Hebrews 2:7 of Christ made lower than the angels.

Greek auxano — to grow, increase; the paired verb of the same verse.

Greek dei — it is necessary, it must be; a divine appointment, not a personal resolve.

Greek philos tou numphiou — the friend of the bridegroom; the office John claims.

Hebrew maat — to be or become few; Psalm 107:38, of cattle not suffered to decrease.

Usage

"“He must increase, but I must decrease” — a divine must, not a resolution."

"“The friend of the bridegroom… rejoiceth greatly” — the joy of the office fulfilled."

"“A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven” — the ground of it all."
